source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 16 (PDF 336-349, printed 336-349); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 16 (Lab Safety and Practical Skills (running header: Identifying Hazards and Designing Safe Experiments)), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 According to the chapter, a chemistry laboratory is described as:
blocks.explanation: 16.1: A chemistry laboratory is a chemist workshop where a student is trained to observe physical and chemical characteristics of substances.

book_ref.quote: A chemistry laboratory is a chemist workshop

blocks.prompt: 2 In the laboratory a student is trained to observe the characteristics of substances by:
blocks.explanation: 16.1: The student observes physical and chemical characteristics by following definite procedures.

book_ref.quote: trained to observe the physical and chemical characteristics of substances by following definite procedures

blocks.prompt: 3 While working in the lab, a student should always wear:

options.text: a lab coat and safety goggles

blocks.explanation: 16.1: Students should always wear a lab coat and safety goggles; girls must tie up their scarves and hair.

book_ref.quote: Students should always wear lab coat and safety goggles while working in the lab

blocks.prompt: 4 Experiments in the lab should be performed:

options.text: in the presence of the lab instructor and other laboratory staff

blocks.explanation: 16.1: Students are advised not to work alone; experiments should be performed in the presence of the lab instructor and staff.

book_ref.quote: Experiments should be performed in the presence of lab instructor and other laboratory staff

blocks.prompt: 5 If a piece of glassware breaks during work, the student should:

options.text: hide the pieces in a drawer
throw the pieces down the drain
continue working and report it next week
report it to the incharge of the laboratory immediately

blocks.explanation: 16.1: Any accident or breakage of glassware must be reported to the incharge immediately.

book_ref.quote: Any accident or breakage of glassware must be reported to the incharge of the laboratory immediately

blocks.prompt: 6 Which practice is NOT allowed in the laboratory?

options.text: keeping a safe distance from others

blocks.explanation: 16.1: Do not pour chemicals down the drains and do not use the sewer for chemical waste disposal.

book_ref.quote: Do not pour chemicals down the drains and do not utilize the sewer for chemical waste disposal

blocks.prompt: 7 The potential hazards of an equipment or experiment should be determined:

options.text: at the end of the session

blocks.explanation: 16.1: Determine the potential hazards before beginning any work; appropriate safety precautions must be observed.

book_ref.quote: Determine the potential hazards related to any equipment or the experiment before beginning any work

blocks.text: 16.2 Common types of hazards in a laboratory

blocks.prompt: 8 Most laboratory hazards fall into how many categories?

options.text: four: physical, chemical, biological and electrical

blocks.explanation: 16.2: Most hazards fall into three categories: physical, chemical and biological hazards.

book_ref.quote: fall into three categories, physical, chemical and biological hazards

blocks.prompt: 9 The most common physical hazards in a laboratory are:

options.text: slips and falls when working on a wet floor

blocks.explanation: 16.2.1: The most common physical hazards are slips and falls on a wet floor.

book_ref.quote: The most common physical hazards are slips and falls when working on wet floor

blocks.prompt: 10 While handling broken glassware, a worker should wear:

options.text: a damp cloth on the hand

blocks.explanation: 16.2.1: Cut-resistant gloves prevent cuts, abrasions and skin damage while handling broken glassware.

book_ref.quote: A worker should wear cut-resistant gloves while handling the broken glassware

blocks.prompt: 11 Broken glassware should be disposed of:
blocks.explanation: 16.2.1: Laboratory staff must dispose of broken glassware in a special container to prevent injury.

book_ref.quote: dispose off broken glassware in special container to prevent injury

blocks.prompt: 12 To avoid chemical hazards, a laboratory worker must use the chemicals:

options.text: in any amount that seems convenient
according to the standard procedures, keeping their particular hazards in view
only when no one is watching

blocks.explanation: 16.2.2: Chemicals must be used according to standard procedures keeping in view their particular hazards and precautions.

book_ref.quote: use the chemicals according to the standard procedures keeping in view the particular hazards

blocks.prompt: 13 Which of these is a biological hazard?

options.text: an infectious disease transferred from animals to humans

blocks.explanation: 16.2.3: The most common biological hazards are allergens, infectious diseases transferred from animals to humans, and viral diseases.

book_ref.quote: infectious diseases which are transferred from animals to humans and viral diseases

blocks.prompt: 14 Slipping, pulling and falling are examples of:
blocks.explanation: 16.2.1: Accidents such as slipping, pulling and falling are related to physical hazards.

book_ref.quote: A worker must take all types of precautions to avoid accidents related to physical hazards

blocks.prompt: 15 Chemical waste should be disposed of according to the rules of:
blocks.explanation: 16.3: Chemical waste cannot go into bins or the sewer; it is disposed of under the rules of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

book_ref.quote: Chemical waste cannot be disposed of in bins or sewer system

blocks.prompt: 16 A chemical waste container should be labelled with:

options.text: only the name of the student
only the colour of the waste
the type of waste, the date and the place of origin

blocks.explanation: 16.3: Containers are labelled with the types of wastes, the date of waste and the place of origin.

book_ref.quote: Label the chemical waste containers with the types of wastes, the date of waste and place of origin

blocks.prompt: 17 Which of the following is NOT listed as a chemical treatment of wastes?
blocks.explanation: 16.3: Chemical treatment of wastes involves neutralization, precipitation, ion exchange, oxidation or reduction; the sewer must not be used.

book_ref.quote: Chemical treatment of wastes involves neutralization, precipitation, ion exchange, oxidation or reduction

blocks.prompt: 18 After storing and labelling, chemical waste containers are:

options.text: transferred to the allocated site for appropriate treatment

blocks.explanation: 16.3: The containers are transferred to the allocated site where they are appropriately treated and disposed of.

book_ref.quote: These containers are then transferred to the allocated site

blocks.prompt: 19 For a minor cut, after removing any glass piece, one should apply:
blocks.explanation: 16.4 (Table 16.1): Methylated spirit or tincture iodine is applied with cotton; both act as disinfectant.

book_ref.quote: apply a little methylated spirit or tincture iodine with a piece of cotton

blocks.prompt: 20 For a serious cut, pressure is applied on the cut for about:
blocks.explanation: 16.4: Apply pressure for about 10 minutes to stop bleeding, then consult a doctor.

book_ref.quote: Apply pressure on the cut for about 10 minutes to stop bleeding

blocks.prompt: 21 If acid goes into the eye, it is washed with water and then with:
blocks.explanation: 16.4: Acid in the eye: wash thoroughly with water and then with 1% sodium bicarbonate solution (a weak base).

book_ref.quote: Wash thoroughly with water and then with 1% sodium bicarbonate solution

blocks.prompt: 22 Alkali in the eye is treated by washing with water followed by:
blocks.explanation: 16.4: Alkali in the eye: wash with water followed by 1% boric acid solution (a weak acid).

book_ref.quote: Wash with water followed by 1% boric acid solution

blocks.prompt: 23 For a foreign particle in the eye, the correct first aid is:

options.text: put a drop of 1% acetic acid
do not rub; remove it with a soft handkerchief and wash with water

blocks.explanation: 16.4: Do not rub the eyes; remove the particle carefully with a soft handkerchief, then wash with water.

book_ref.quote: Do not rub the eyes. Remove the particle carefully with soft handkerchief then wash with water.

blocks.prompt: 24 Soreness in the eye is relieved by:

options.text: a drop of olive oil, keeping the eyes closed for some time

blocks.explanation: 16.4: Put a drop of olive oil in the eyes and keep them closed for some time.

book_ref.quote: Put a drop of olive oil in the eyes and keep them closed for some time.

blocks.prompt: 25 An alkali burn is washed with water and then with:
blocks.explanation: 16.4: an alkali burn is neutralised with a weak acid: wash with water, then 1% acetic acid, again water, dry and apply burnol.

book_ref.quote: Wash freely with water and then with 1% acetic acid solution and again with water, dry the skin and apply the burnol.

blocks.prompt: 26 A bromine burn is treated with:

options.text: 2% ammonia solution, then glycerin and later burnol

blocks.explanation: 16.4: bromine burns: wash with 2% ammonia solution and apply glycerin, then burnol.

book_ref.quote: Wash fully with 2% ammonia solution and apply glycerin.

blocks.prompt: 27 A burn caused by dry heat (a flame or hot object) is treated by applying:
blocks.explanation: 16.4: burns with dry heat: apply burnol or mustard oil.

book_ref.quote: Apply burnol or mustard oil.

blocks.prompt: 28 If an acid is swallowed, the person should drink a lot of water or:

options.text: lime water or milk of magnesia

blocks.explanation: 16.4: Acid swallowed: drink a lot of water or lime water or milk of magnesia.

book_ref.quote: Drink a lot of water or lime water or milk of magnesia.

blocks.prompt: 29 If a caustic alkali is swallowed, the person should drink a lot of water and then:

options.text: a glass of lemon or orange juice

blocks.explanation: 16.4: Caustic alkalies swallowed: drink a lot of water and a glass of lemon or orange juice.

book_ref.quote: Drink a lot of water; drink a glass of lemon or orange juice.

blocks.prompt: 30 When a salt of a heavy metal is swallowed, the first aid is to take:

options.text: milk or the white part of an egg

blocks.explanation: 16.4: Salts of heavy metals swallowed: take milk or the white part of the egg.

book_ref.quote: Take milk or white part of the egg.

blocks.prompt: 31 A beaker of inflammable liquid catches fire. Covering it with a damp cloth puts out the fire because it:

options.text: cuts off the supply of oxygen

blocks.explanation: 16.4: Covering the beaker with a duster or damp cloth cuts off the supply of oxygen.

book_ref.quote: Cover the beaker with a duster or damp cloth. This will cut off the supply of oxygen.

blocks.prompt: 32 Burning spirit or oil should be put out with:

options.text: a mixture of sand and sodium bicarbonate
a wet sponge squeezed over it

blocks.explanation: 16.4: Throw a mixture of sand and sodium bicarbonate; water will simply spread the fire.

book_ref.quote: Throw a mixture of sand and sodium bicarbonate. Do not throw water. It will simply spread the fire.

blocks.prompt: 33 When electric parts catch fire, the first step is to:

options.text: cover them with a wet blanket while the supply is on
switch off the electric supply and throw sand

blocks.explanation: 16.4: Switch off the electric supply immediately and throw sand; never use water.

book_ref.quote: Switch off the electric supply immediately and throw sand.

blocks.prompt: 34 If a person's clothes catch fire, he should:

options.text: not run; wrap himself in a blanket and lie down on the floor
run outside to the open air

blocks.explanation: 16.4: Do not run; wrap with a blanket or dry cotton cloth and lie down on the floor.

book_ref.quote: Do not run. Wrap with blanket or with dry cotton cloth. Lie down on the floor.

blocks.prompt: 35 Volumetric analysis finds the concentrations of solutions by a technique called:
blocks.explanation: 16.5: Volumetric analysis finds concentrations of solutions by titration.

book_ref.quote: Volumetric analysis is used to find the concentrations of solutions by means of a technique known as titration

blocks.prompt: 36 A substance that shows the completion of a reaction by a change in its colour is called:
blocks.explanation: 16.5: The substance which indicates the completion of reaction by the change in its colour is called an indicator.

book_ref.quote: The substance which indicates the completion of reaction by the change in its colour is called an indicator.

blocks.prompt: 37 The moment at which the indicator changes colour is called the:
blocks.explanation: 16.5: The moment at which the indicator changes colour is called the end point.

book_ref.quote: The moment at which the indicator changes colour is called the end point.

blocks.prompt: 38 In an acid-base titration, which solution is taken in the burette?

options.text: only the acid, never the base
only the base, never the acid
either solution, with the other in a conical (titration) flask

blocks.explanation: 16.5: Either solution can be taken in the burette, with the other in a conical or titration flask.

book_ref.quote: Either solution can be taken in a burette with the other solution taken in a conical or a titration flask.

blocks.prompt: 39 Phenolphthalein solution is made with 1 g of indicator in 500 cm³ of 50% ethanol. How much indicator is needed for 250 cm³ of the same solution?
blocks.explanation: 16.5 (Did you know): 1 g per 500 cm³, so 250 cm³ needs 1 × 250/500 = 0.5 g.

book_ref.quote: Phenolphthalein solution is prepared by adding one gram of the indicator in 500 cm³ of 50% ethanol.

blocks.prompt: 40 Phenolphthalein changes colour from pink to colourless when the pH:
blocks.explanation: 16.5 (Did you know): The colour change is from pink to colourless as the pH decreases.

book_ref.quote: The color change is from pink to colorless as the pH decreases.

blocks.prompt: 41 The light pink colour at the end point fades gradually because of:

options.text: atmospheric carbon dioxide slowly dissolving in the solution

blocks.explanation: 16.5: The light pink colour fades due to interference of atmospheric CO₂, which slowly dissolves in the solution.

book_ref.quote: tends to fade gradually due to the interference of atmospheric carbon dioxide

blocks.prompt: 42 Which of these is NOT listed among the materials for the HCl-NaOH titration?
blocks.explanation: 16.5 Materials: burette, pipette, funnel, conical flask, HCl, NaOH and phenolphthalein; no burner is needed.

book_ref.quote: Burette, pipette, funnel, conical flask, HCl solution, NaOH solution, phenolphthalein.

blocks.prompt: 43 The products of the reaction between NaOH(aq) and HCl(aq) are:
blocks.explanation: 16.5: NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l).

book_ref.quote: No. of moles of the base in the balanced chemical equation

blocks.prompt: 44 Before the titration, the conical flask is rinsed with:
blocks.explanation: 16.5 Procedure: Rinse the conical flask with distilled water only (the pipette and burette are rinsed with their own solutions after water).

book_ref.quote: Rinse the conical flask with distilled water only.

blocks.prompt: 45 In this titration the pipette is rinsed first with distilled water and then with:
blocks.explanation: 16.5 Procedure: Rinse the pipette with distilled water and then with the NaOH solution it will measure.

book_ref.quote: Rinse the pipette first with distilled water and then with the given NaOH solution.

blocks.prompt: 46 Some acid is run from the burette into a beaker before titrating in order to:

options.text: remove any air bubble present in the nozzle
check the colour of the acid

blocks.explanation: 16.5 Procedure: Acid is allowed to flow into a beaker to remove any air bubble in the nozzle.

book_ref.quote: allow the acid to flow into a beaker to remove any air bubble present in the nozzle

blocks.prompt: 47 The initial burette reading is noted using:

options.text: an anti-parallax card or a white paper

blocks.explanation: 16.5 Procedure: The initial reading is noted using an anti-parallax card or white paper.

book_ref.quote: Note the burette reading as an initial reading using an anti-parallax card or a white paper.

blocks.prompt: 48 During titration the conical flask is placed on a white paper so that:

options.text: the colour change of the indicator is seen clearly

blocks.explanation: 16.5 Procedure: A white paper under the flask lets the colour change be seen clearly.

book_ref.quote: place the conical flask on a white paper under the burette to see the color change

blocks.prompt: 49 NaOH with phenolphthalein is in the flask and HCl is added from the burette. At the end point the solution:
blocks.explanation: 16.5 (Book correction): with NaOH in the flask and acid added, the pink colour just disappears at the end point.

book_ref.quote: pink colour just disappears and the solution becomes colourless

blocks.prompt: 50 When one or two drops of phenolphthalein are added to the NaOH solution in the flask, the solution turns:
blocks.explanation: 16.5 Procedure: The NaOH solution turns pink with phenolphthalein.

book_ref.quote: Add one to two drops of phenolphthalein indicator into it. The solution turns pink.

blocks.prompt: 51 The initial burette reading is 1.20 cm³ and the final reading is 11.70 cm³. The volume of acid used is:
blocks.explanation: 16.5: Volume used = final − initial = 11.70 − 1.20 = 10.50 cm³.

book_ref.quote: The difference of final and initial readings of burette will give the volume of the acid used.

blocks.prompt: 52 Four titre volumes are 12.40, 12.45, 12.50 and 12.95 cm³. Which reading is NOT concordant with the others?
blocks.explanation: 16.5: Concordant readings agree within 0.1 cm³; 12.40, 12.45 and 12.50 agree, but 12.95 differs by about 0.5 cm³.

book_ref.quote: Take at least three concordant readings which agree with one another within 0.1 cm³.

blocks.prompt: 53 The first (rough) titration is carried out by adding the acid from the burette:

options.text: with the funnel still in the burette
drop wise, swirling the flask for thorough mixing

blocks.explanation: 16.5 Procedure: Acid is added drop wise and the flask is swirled for thorough mixing.

book_ref.quote: Carry out a rough titration by adding hydrochloric acid solution from the burette drop wise

blocks.prompt: 54 In the molarity equation M₁V₁/n₁ = M₂V₂/n₂, the symbol n₁ stands for:

options.text: the number of moles of the acid in the balanced chemical equation

blocks.explanation: 16.5 Calculation: n₁ = number of moles of the acid in the balanced chemical equation.

book_ref.quote: n₁ = No. of moles of the acid in the balanced chemical equation

blocks.prompt: 55 10 cm³ of NaOH solution needs 15.0 cm³ of 0.20 M HCl for neutralisation (1:1 reaction). The molarity of the NaOH solution is:

book_ref.quote: Find out the molarity of NaOH solution by using the following molarity equation:

blocks.prompt: 56 In the observation table, if x is the final reading and y the initial reading, the volume of acid used is:
blocks.explanation: 16.5 Observations: volume of acid used = (x − y).

book_ref.quote: Volume of acid used (cm³)

blocks.prompt: 57 A solid sample gives brisk effervescence with dilute HCl, and the gas turns lime water milky. The anion is:
blocks.explanation: 16.6 (a): Carbonate gives CO₂ with dilute HCl; CO₂ turns lime water milky (CaCO₃).

book_ref.quote: Effervescence takes place during which a gas evolves briskly

blocks.prompt: 58 Lime water turns milky with CO₂ because of the formation of:
blocks.explanation: 16.6: Ca(OH)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s) (white ppt) + H₂O(l).

book_ref.quote: Pass the gas evolved in the above step through a solution of lime water

blocks.prompt: 59 An acidified salt solution gives a thick white precipitate with AgNO₃ which dissolves in aqueous NH₃. The ion present is:
blocks.explanation: 16.6 (b): A thick white precipitate (AgCl) soluble in aqueous NH₃ indicates Cl¹⁻.

book_ref.quote: A thick white precipitate is formed which dissolves in aq.NH₃.

blocks.prompt: 60 With acidified AgNO₃ solution, bromide ions give:

options.text: a bright yellow precipitate of AgI
a thick cream-yellow precipitate of AgBr
a white precipitate soluble in NH₃
a heavy white precipitate of BaSO₄

blocks.explanation: 16.6 (b): Br¹⁻ gives a thick cream-yellow precipitate, AgBr.

book_ref.quote: A thick cream-yellow precipitate is formed.

blocks.prompt: 61 A bright yellow precipitate with acidified AgNO₃ solution indicates:
blocks.explanation: 16.6 (b): Iodide gives a bright yellow precipitate of AgI.

book_ref.quote: A bright yellow precipitate is formed.

blocks.prompt: 62 In the tests for halide ions, dilute HNO₃ is added before AgNO₃ in order to:

options.text: prevent the precipitation of carbonate ions along with halide ions
provide nitrate ions for the test

blocks.explanation: 16.6 (Did you know): Dilute nitric acid prevents carbonate ions from precipitating along with halide ions.

book_ref.quote: dilute nitric acid is added to prevent the precipitation of carbonate ions

blocks.prompt: 63 In the test for nitrate ions, the salt solution is treated with NaOH solution and:
blocks.explanation: 16.6 (c): NaOH solution and powdered aluminium are added; NH₃ gas is given off.

book_ref.quote: Finally add 3 g of powdered aluminium metal.

blocks.prompt: 64 In the nitrate test, the gas evolved near the mouth of the test tube:

options.text: is NH₃ and turns red litmus blue
is CO₂ and turns lime water milky
is NO₂ and turns blue litmus red
is H₂ and burns with a pop

blocks.explanation: 16.6 (c): NH₃ gas with a characteristic smell turns red litmus paper blue.

book_ref.quote: A characteristic smell of NH₃ gas is felt near the mouth of test tube.

blocks.prompt: 65 In the nitrate test, aluminium metal acts as:

options.text: a reducing agent that is itself oxidised

blocks.explanation: 16.6 (Book correction): No cell is involved; Al is the reducing agent, oxidised to [Al(OH)₄]¹⁻, and reduces NO₃¹⁻ to NH₃.

book_ref.quote: It is the reducing agent: it is itself oxidised

blocks.prompt: 66 In the balanced equation for the reduction of nitrate by aluminium, how many moles of Al react with 3 moles of NO₃¹⁻?
blocks.explanation: 16.6: 3NO₃¹⁻ + 8Al + 5OH⁻ + 18H₂O → 3NH₃ + 8[Al(OH)₄]¹⁻.

book_ref.quote: reduces nitrate ions to ammonium ions which then react with aqueous NaOH

blocks.prompt: 67 An acidified salt solution gives a heavy white precipitate with barium nitrate solution. The anion is:
blocks.explanation: 16.6 (d): SO₄²⁻ + Ba²⁺ → BaSO₄(s), a heavy white precipitate.

book_ref.quote: A heavy white precipitate of BaSO₄ is formed.

blocks.prompt: 68 In the sulphate test, the solution is acidified with dilute HNO₃ to:

options.text: destroy any carbonate ions present as an impurity

blocks.explanation: 16.6 (Did you know): Dilute HNO₃ destroys carbonate ions present as an impurity.

book_ref.quote: Dilute nitric acid is added to destroy any carbonate ions present in the solution as an impurity.

blocks.text: 16.7 Tests for identification of basic radicals

blocks.prompt: 69 A salt solution gives a white gelatinous precipitate with NaOH solution and a white precipitate with a few drops of aqueous ammonia. The cation (as described in 16.7 a) is:
blocks.explanation: 16.7 (a): Al³⁺ gives a white gelatinous Al(OH)₃ precipitate with NaOH and a white precipitate with aqueous ammonia.

book_ref.quote: A white gelatinous precipitate is formed.

blocks.prompt: 70 A salt warmed gently with NaOH solution gives a gas with a distinct smell that turns moist red litmus blue. The cation is:
blocks.explanation: 16.7 (b): NH₄¹⁺ + OH¹⁻ → NH₃(g) + H₂O(l); ammonia turns moist red litmus blue.

book_ref.quote: Add NaOH solution and gently heat it.

blocks.prompt: 71 With NaOH solution, Ca²⁺ ions give:

options.text: a white precipitate insoluble in excess NaOH
a white precipitate soluble in excess NaOH

blocks.explanation: 16.7 (c): Ca²⁺ gives white Ca(OH)₂ which does not dissolve in excess NaOH.

book_ref.quote: White precipitate is formed which does not dissolve in excess of NaOH solution.

blocks.prompt: 72 With aqueous ammonia, a solution of Ca²⁺ ions gives:

options.text: only a slight turbidity or no precipitate

blocks.explanation: 16.7 (c): With aqueous ammonia only a slight turbidity appears, or no precipitate forms.

book_ref.quote: Only a slight turbidity appears or No precipitate is formed.

blocks.prompt: 73 A green precipitate forms with NaOH and turns into a green solution in excess NaOH. It is also insoluble in excess aqueous ammonia. The ion is:
blocks.explanation: 16.7 (d): Cr³⁺ gives green Cr(OH)₃, which forms a green solution in excess NaOH and is insoluble in excess ammonia.

book_ref.quote: A green precipitate appears which turns into green solution when excess of NaOH is added

blocks.prompt: 74 With aqueous ammonia, a solution of Cu²⁺ ions forms:
blocks.explanation: 16.7 (e): Cu²⁺ with aqueous ammonia gives a deep blue solution.

book_ref.quote: Deep blue solution is formed.

blocks.prompt: 75 The light-blue precipitate formed when NaOH solution is added to a Cu²⁺ solution is:
blocks.explanation: 16.7 (e): Cu²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Cu(OH)₂(s), a blue precipitate.

book_ref.quote: A light-blue precipitate is formed.

blocks.prompt: 76 Fe³⁺ ions give an orange brown precipitate with both NaOH and aqueous ammonia. The precipitate is:
blocks.explanation: 16.7 (f): Fe³⁺ + 3OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₃(s), orange brown precipitate.

book_ref.quote: Take 2 g FeCl₃ in a clean test tube.

blocks.prompt: 77 With NaOH solution, Fe²⁺ ions give a precipitate that:

options.text: is orange brown from the start
is green and turns orange brown after some time
is white and dissolves in excess NaOH

blocks.explanation: 16.7 (f): Fe²⁺ gives green Fe(OH)₂, which turns orange brown after some time.

book_ref.quote: A green precipitate is formed which is turned into orange brown precipitate after some time.

blocks.prompt: 78 The white gelatinous Fe(OH)₂ formed with aqueous ammonia changes to red brown Fe(OH)₃ because it is:
blocks.explanation: 16.7 (f): Fe(OH)₂ quickly oxidizes to red brown Fe(OH)₃.

book_ref.quote: quickly oxidizes to form red brown precipitate of Fe(OH)₃

blocks.prompt: 79 A cation gives a white precipitate with NaOH that dissolves in excess NaOH, and a white precipitate with aqueous ammonia that dissolves in excess ammonia. The cation is:
blocks.explanation: 16.7 (g): Zn(OH)₂ is soluble in excess NaOH and in excess ammonia.

book_ref.quote: White precipitate is formed which dissolves in excess of ammonia.

blocks.prompt: 80 The white precipitate formed by Zn²⁺ ions with hydroxide ions is:
blocks.explanation: 16.7 (g): Zn²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Zn(OH)₂(s), white ppt.

book_ref.quote: White precipitate is formed which is soluble in excess of NaOH solution.
